intro.title: The garden's season
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Welcome to the capstone quest. Each one is a full piece of work on data of its own, using skills from across the course: reading and cleaning, grouping and joining, a test where it helps, and a short report at the end. The challenges say what the result should look like, not how to get it, so there is usually more than one good answer; the hints show one way.

The first is the Elm Street community garden. Every week the gardeners weigh what they pick and write it on a shared sheet, which has the usual problems: plot letters in either case, crops spelled three ways, weights written with "kg", and one weigh-in left blank. There is also a small table of which family looks after which plot.

```
raw <- "date,plot,crop,weight
03/06/2026,A,Tomatoes,2.4kg
03/06/2026,b,beans,1.1 kg
10/06/2026,A,tomatoes,3.0kg
10/06/2026,C,Kale,0.8kg
17/06/2026,B,Beans,1.6kg
17/06/2026,C,kale,
01/07/2026,A,tomatoes,4.2kg
01/07/2026,B,beans,2.0kg
08/07/2026,C,kale,1.2kg
08/07/2026,A,Tomatoes,3.8kg
15/07/2026,b,BEANS,1.9kg
15/07/2026,C,kale,1.5kg"
plots <- data.frame(plot = c("A", "B", "C"), family = c("Silva", "Okafor", "Li"))
```

At the end of the season the garden committee wants to know how much each crop and each family produced, how the months compare, and whether the new leaf-mould compost was worth it. Each challenge starts from the steps before it, so you can check one step at a time.

challenges.title: Expert: Was the compost worth it?
challenges.promptMarkdown: In a side trial, 6 beds had home compost and 6 leaf mould. Make `p` the p-value of a t-test of kg by compost, rounded to 3 decimal places, and `gain` the leaf-mould mean minus the home mean, rounded to 2.
challenges.hint: `t.test(kg ~ compost, data = trial)$p.value`; the means are in `$estimate` (home first, alphabetically), or use `tapply()`.
challenges.solution:
trial <- data.frame(
  compost = rep(c("home", "leaf"), each = 6),
  kg = c(2.1, 2.6, 1.9, 2.4, 2.2, 2.0, 2.7, 3.1, 2.5, 2.9, 3.3, 2.6)
)
res <- t.test(kg ~ compost, data = trial)
p <- round(res$p.value, 3)
gain <- round(unname(res$estimate[2] - res$estimate[1]), 2)

intro.title: Plan your own analysis
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The best way to keep learning is to analyse data you care about: your sports club's results, your own step counts, prices you track, a school survey. This last capstone is about **how** to do that well, in small, checkable steps. The challenges walk through the process on an example, a library's daily visitor counts for four weeks, so you can use the same steps on your own data.

**1. Write the question first.** One sentence: "Which days is the library busiest, and is the weekend really quieter?" A clear question tells you which columns matter and when you are done.

**2. Look before you count.** `str()`, `summary()` and `table()` show the types, the range and the odd values. Here a count of −1 and an NA stand out straight away.

```
visits <- data.frame(
  date = seq(as.Date("2026-09-07"), by = "day", length.out = 28),
  visitors = c(112, 98, 105, 120, 134, 76, 41, 108, 95, -1, 118, 140, 81, 38,
               115, 101, 99, NA, 129, 72, 45, 110, 92, 104, 116, 138, 79, 40)
)
summary(visits$visitors)
```

**3. Put checking and cleaning in functions.** A function like `check_visits()` that lists the problems, and `clean_visits()` that fixes them, can be run again on next month's data with one call, and you can test them.

**4. Test on a tiny example you can work out by hand.** If `clean_visits()` turns `c(5, -1, 7)` into `c(5, NA, 7)`, you can trust it on the real data. `stopifnot()` stops with an error the moment a check is FALSE.

**5. Summarise, compare, then report.** Group summaries answer most questions; a test tells you whether a difference is bigger than chance. Write the report as a function that **returns** its lines, so it can be checked and reused, and say what was left out.

Then take your own data through the same steps: question, look, check, clean, test, summarise, report.
